content.thinking:
I need to write the postmortem without inserting any actual figures myself, using placeholders like {duration} and {began} instead. Labels such as T2, C1, or AI-2 are fine, but I should avoid specific hardware names with digits like "A100" or "V100," opting instead for a generic description like "the newer accelerator card."

For the symptom description, I should describe it simply as "orders were flagged for fraud holds more often" without citing numbers, referencing the FraudHoldsHigh alert. Then I'll build out the causal chain: the fraud-hold series rose while error rates stayed flat, pointing to the fraud scorer behaving differently on a new pod, which traces back to replicas being placed on a different accelerator type at onset without pinning — all tied to evidence labels like T1, T6, T7, and Gd066.

Root cause is that pods weren't constrained to a specific accelerator type, so the scheduler placed a new replica on a different GPU model whose scorer output diverged from the others; I'm treating the model-behavior mechanism as inferred but the mitigation (pinning to older cards) is confirmed by the recovery timing lining up closely with the action taken. I'm noting contributing factors — no accelerator constraint, no alerting on mixed accelerator types or scorer divergence, and no pre-release verification on new hardware — and drafting action items (AI-2 through AI-3+) including making the accelerator constraint permanent and reviewing the fix PR whose contents I don't actually know yet.

I'm flagging that error-rate-based alerting wouldn't have caught this since the error rate never rose, and the alert title is misleading, so I'm drafting action items: AI-3 pin accelerator type permanently in the pod spec and verify it's declarative, AI-4 add detection for replicas running on mismatched accelerator models or diverging scorer output, AI-5 require validation of the fraud model on new hardware before node pool rollout, and possibly AI-6 fix the alert text — trying to keep this to 3-4 items. For lessons learned, I'm noting the fast 2-minute response after alert as a win, but the hold wasn't applied until several minutes of impact had passed, and we got lucky that the error rate didn't spike since that's the only thing being monitored; I'm also noting C2 was never attempted, and starting to draft an executive summary of the incident timeline and duration.

action_items.item: Make the accelerator constraint permanent in the io-shop deployment spec, using a node selector or affinity for the validated card type. Confirm that rescheduling and scale-up cannot place pods on other models.
Before any new accelerator model is allowed for io-shop, run the fraud scorer on it and compare its outputs and hold rate with the current card. Admit the model only if they are equivalent.

Add a check that alerts when replicas of one service run on different accelerator models. Also compare the fraud-hold rate per replica so a single divergent replica is visible. Correct the FraudHoldsHigh alert description so it does not say 'error rate'.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw the fraud-hold measure that paged rise from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average, peaking at {series_at_worst}, from {began} until {recovered}. Request failures did not rise: the error rate was {errors_before} before and {errors_while_broken} during. So the harm was altered fraud-scoring outcomes (probably extra fraud holds), not failed pages.

The fraud scorer on a newly started replica answered differently from the other replicas. The log shows it serving on the newer accelerator card at the minute the measure stepped up, and only that replica was on the new card.

The new replica started on a different accelerator model from the other two replicas, which run on the older card. Nothing constrained the service to one card type, as the mitigation record shows the pods were held to no card.

No deploy, release, config or flag change explains the shift. The change log and flag history were empty, so the trigger was ordinary scheduling placing a replica on available hardware, not a change by anyone.

Holding the pods to the older card type was followed by the measure returning to baseline and the rule that paged stopping. This supports accelerator type as the cause, although the model-level reason for the different answers was not investigated.

contributing_factors.factor: The accelerator type is not part of the service's declared requirements, so the scheduler may mix card models. The hold applied during the incident is a mitigation and is not yet a lasting rule.
Nothing checks that the fraud-scoring model gives equivalent results on every accelerator model it might run on. A different card changed its behaviour unnoticed.

Detection relied on a downstream fraud-hold quality measure. The alert text says 'error rate', yet request errors were flat, and nothing flagged mixed card types across replicas at the onset. The alert fired only after the onset.
The proposed code fix has not been reviewed. How it relates to the accelerator placement is unclear from the record.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, the shop's fraud-hold measure ran well above its usual level. It averaged {series_while_broken} against {series_before} beforehand and peaked at {series_at_worst}. Requests did not fail more than normal. The error rate stayed near its usual level, so pages loaded and orders went through. The change was in how the fraud scoring behaved, so some shoppers were probably held for fraud review when they would not normally have been. A new copy of the service had started on a different type of accelerator card from the other copies, and the fraud model answers differently on it. Argus restricted the service to the older card type. The measure returned to baseline and the alert stopped firing. Argus held the incident for {held}. A draft fix has been proposed and is awaiting review.

got_lucky: Request errors, latency and volume stayed at baseline, so the fault affected only fraud scoring and nothing failed outright.
Only one of three replicas was on the new card. If more replicas had been rescheduled onto it, a larger share of scoring could have shifted.
went_well: Argus took the alert, built two candidate causes and acted within seconds. The leading candidate was tied to a replica placement and a log line at the onset.
The mitigation was narrow and reversible, and its effect was checked against the metrics before it was judged confirmed.
went_wrong: The service could be placed on mixed accelerator models, and nothing flagged that until the quality measure moved.
The fraud-hold measure was elevated for {duration} before recovery. The impact was a change in scoring outcomes, which the error-rate and latency series could not show.
The alert text described an error rate although request errors never rose, which is misleading for whoever is paged.

input.root_cause: The shop's pods were not restricted to one accelerator model. At {began} the scheduler placed a new replica on a different, newer GPU model than the two serving replicas. The fraud-scoring model gives different answers on that card, and fraud holds rose even though no deploy or config change had landed.
input.symptom: Fraud holds ran higher than normal
